meta.ogDescription: Verified word for word in the State Department's own transcript of Colin Powell's 5 February 2003 UN address. Real quote, false claim — here's the record.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Powell said this from the floor of the UN Security Council in New York City on 5 February 2003, in the address titled “Remarks to the United Nations Security Council.” The wording is exact — it matches the State Department’s own official transcript word for word. What did not survive scrutiny was the claim itself.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Remarks to the United Nations Security Council
Official, U.S. Department of State archive

source.excerpt:
Iraq admitted to producing four spray tanks, but to this day, it has provided no credible evidence that they were destroyed, evidence that was required by the international community.

There can be no doubt that Saddam Hussein has biological weapons and the capability to rapidly produce more, many more. And he has the ability to dispense these lethal poisons and diseases in ways that can cause massive death and destruction.

If biological weapons seem too terrible to contemplate, chemical weapons are equally chilling.
trail: Searched Quote Investigator first — it has no entry for this line, so there is no specialist finding to defer to. Wikiquote ↗ carries it among Powell’s sourced quotations, cited to the Security Council remarks of 5 February 2003.

Went to the primary record: the U.S. Department of State’s archived official transcript ↗, headed “Remarks to the United Nations Security Council · Secretary Colin L. Powell · New York City · February 5, 2003,” which contains the sentence word for word.

Confirmed the same wording independently in the American Presidency Project transcript ↗ and in the National Security Archive’s scan of the address ↗. Three independent transcripts, no variant readings.
Checked what happened to the claim: the Iraq Survey Group found no biological or chemical weapons stockpiles ↗, and Powell himself later called the speech a blot on his record ↗.
source.excerptNote: Text as printed in the U.S. Department of State’s archived transcript. The line sits at the close of the biological-weapons portion of the address, immediately before Powell turns to chemical weapons.

source.rightsNote: Powell spoke these words as Secretary of State in his official capacity, and the transcript quoted here is the State Department’s own. Under 17 U.S.C. § 105 ↗, copyright protection “is not available for any work of the United States Government” — defined as a work prepared by a U.S. Government officer or employee as part of their official duties — so the address is in the public domain despite its 2003 date. That exemption covers the government’s own transcript; commercial news transcriptions of the same speech may carry their own rights.

author.name: Colin Powell
author.kicker: The man who made the case
author.heading: About Colin Powell
author.metaLine: 1937–2021 · U.S. Secretary of State and four-star general
author.bio: Colin Powell (1937–2021) was a four-star U.S. Army general who served as National Security Advisor from 1987 to 1989 and as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff from 1989 to 1993 before becoming Secretary of State from January 2001 to January 2005. He was, by some distance, the most trusted figure in the administration he served — which is precisely why he was sent to the Security Council to make the case for war. He spent much of the rest of his life answering for the twenty minutes in which he made it, calling the speech a “blot” on his record that was “painful” then and “painful now.”

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: This is the rare case where the correction runs backwards. Nobody has to rescue this quote from a fake attribution — it is Powell’s, verbatim, on the record, in a transcript his own department published. What collapsed was everything the sentence asserted, and that is where the misunderstandings actually live.

items.why: Not a paraphrase, not a press summary, not a line someone else wrote and Powell was blamed for. It appears word for word in the State Department’s official transcript ↗ of “Remarks to the United Nations Security Council,” New York City, 5 February 2003.

items.who: Refuted by the Iraq Survey Group
items.why: The Survey Group reported that Iraq appears to have destroyed its biological weapons and agent in 1991–1992, with research abandoned by 1996, and found no biological or chemical weapons stockpiles ↗ in 2003.
Rafid Ahmed Alwan al-Janabi, the Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball, supplied the mobile biological-laboratory claims that fed the presentation and later admitted he had lied ↗.
In Cairo on 24 February 2001, alongside Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, Powell said Saddam Hussein “has not developed any significant capability with respect to weapons of mass destruction” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: He said it, exactly as quoted, and he did not hide from it: Powell told Barbara Walters of ABC News in 2005 that the speech was a blot on his record — “It was painful. It is painful now.” ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Powell was sent to the Security Council because he was the one member of the administration the world might believe. He had been a soldier for thirty-five years, he had a reputation for caution, and he was widely understood to be the reluctant one in the room. The speech was built to trade on exactly that credibility — intercepted phone calls played aloud, satellite photographs, a vial held up to the cameras — and this sentence was its hinge: not a warning about intent or capability at some future date, but a flat declaration in the present tense that the weapons existed.

The certainty was borrowed, and the loan was bad. Much of the biological-weapons material traced back to an Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball ↗, who later admitted he had made it up. When the Iraq Survey Group finished its work, it reported that Iraq had destroyed its biological weapons around 1991–1992 and that the trailers seized after the invasion — presented before the war as mobile production labs — “have absolutely nothing to do with any biological weapons” ↗.
context.detailsSummary: The sentence in its place in the speech
detailsBody: The line closes Powell’s biological-weapons section. It follows a passage about Iraqi spray tanks and a Mirage jet test flight, and it is immediately followed by the pivot into chemical weapons: “If biological weapons seem too terrible to contemplate, chemical weapons are equally chilling.”

In February 2001, standing in Cairo beside Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, Powell had said of Saddam Hussein that “he has not developed any significant capability with respect to weapons of mass destruction” ↗. In February 2003 he told the Security Council there could be no doubt that the weapons were there.
context.pull: The attribution is airtight. That is the whole problem with it.

sourcesVerified.claim: The State Department's official archived transcript, headed 'Remarks to the United Nations Security Council / Secretary Colin L. Powell / New York City / February 5, 2003', contains the sentence verbatim.

The American Presidency Project transcript, titled 'Address by Secretary of State Colin Powell to the United Nations Security Council', dated February 05, 2003, New York, contains the sentence verbatim followed by 'And he has the ability to dispense these lethal poisons and diseases in ways that can cause massive death and destruction.'
The National Security Archive's PDF transcript of the 5 February 2003 address, which includes the presentation slides, contains the sentence verbatim.
Wikiquote lists the quote among Colin Powell's sourced quotations (2000s section, not Disputed or Misattributed), cited to 'Remarks to the United Nations Security Council (5 February 2003)'.
The Iraq Survey Group concluded Iraq did not have biological or chemical weapons stockpiles in 2003, and found no evidence of biological warfare programme plans after 1996.

The Duelfer Report concluded Iraq appears to have destroyed its biological weapons and agent in 1991-1992, and that the trailers seized after the invasion 'have absolutely nothing to do with any biological weapons'.
Colin Powell told Barbara Walters of ABC News in 2005 that the UN speech was a blot on his record: 'It was painful. It is painful now.'
On 24 February 2001 in Cairo, alongside Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, Powell said Saddam Hussein 'has not developed any significant capability with respect to weapons of mass destruction.'

Rafid Ahmed Alwan al-Janabi, codenamed Curveball, claimed to have built mobile biological weapons laboratories for Iraq, his claims influenced Powell's 5 February 2003 UN presentation, and he admitted in February 2011 that he had lied.

Colin Powell was born 5 April 1937, died 18 October 2021, served as National Security Advisor 1987-1989, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff 1989-1993, and Secretary of State January 2001 to January 2005, holding the rank of four-star general.

17 U.S.C. 105(a) states copyright protection is not available for any work of the United States Government, defined in section 101 as a work prepared by an officer or employee of the U.S. Government as part of that person's official duties.

Powell's presentation took place on February 5, 2003 at the United Nations Security Council in Manhattan, New York City, and he later characterised it as a lasting blot on his record and a great intelligence failure.
